repos.title: StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Decision Models with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions
repos.paper_summary: StartLux-Decision is a family of 0.8B–27B decision models that output probability distributions over candidate options for typed questions. The Instant variant makes one forward pass with bidirectional attention in its full-attention layers. The AutoThink variant first makes a one-pass prediction, then generates a reasoning trace of up to 4,096 tokens only when its top probability is below 0.9, and averages the initial and post-reasoning distributions. The final training stage adds reasoning supervision and RLCD2, which uses a frozen reference model, proper-score rewards, and a soft length penalty. RLCD2 raises the share of traces that finish within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points and cuts average reasoning length by up to 65%, with accuracy largely preserved. On the public Decision Index 0.3 subset, Instant models beat the strongest comparable-scale open-weight decision models by 7.4–16.9 points, and the 27B AutoThink reaches 73.4. On DecisionPivot, a programmatically generated benchmark of contrast pairs, AutoThink beats its Instant counterpart by 11.5–18.4 points in pair accuracy. Policy-aware calibration reduces confidence–accuracy gaps to within 2.7 points across 184 settings. Stated limitations include generalization beyond represented task families and reliability under distribution shift, both left to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Decision models need reasoning on hard cases without losing single-pass efficiency; the paper proposes two variants, RLCD2 training, and DecisionPivot.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Design and Training
digest_headlines.headline: Three-stage training gives Instant bidirectional attention and teaches AutoThink to reason only when its confidence is below 0.9.

digest_headlines.heading: RLCD2: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions
digest_headlines.headline: RLCD2 rewards reasoning by the change in proper score and penalizes traces beyond a soft budget.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On the public Decision Index 0.3 subset, Instant models lead comparable-scale references by 7.4–16.9 points.

digest_headlines.heading: Capability and Reliability Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Selecting among candidates makes reported confidence overconfident, and policy-aware calibration narrows the gaps across 184 settings.

digest_headlines.heading: Efficient Inference and Deployment
digest_headlines.headline: Single-pass Instant readouts on a single GPU take 24–52 ms for 256-token prompts and 31–98 ms for 1,024-token prompts.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Future work targets generalization beyond represented task families and reliability under distribution shift.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix documents training data sources and decontamination, policy-aware calibration proofs, and serving configuration safeguards.

repos.title: Constraint Breeds Generalization: Temporal Dynamics as an Inductive Bias
repos.paper_summary: This paper argues that dissipative temporal dynamics, meaning phase-space contraction, act as an inductive bias that improves generalization in spiking neural networks (SNNs). Static features are converted into time series by a Duffing oscillator whose parameter δ sets the dynamics as expansive (δ<0), transition (δ≈0 to 2), or dissipative. Leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with leak β provide an architecture-level variant. On handwritten digits (64 features, 10 classes), SNNs trained in the transition regime generalize across a 12×12 matrix of encodings, while expansive-trained networks fail outside their training encoding. On CIFAR-10 patches, the transition regime yields localized, oriented receptive fields (structure score 0.206, versus 0.0541 for the best alternative in Table 1). Experiment 3 reports zero-shot transfer to unseen physical environments in reinforcement learning that beats baseline architectures. Limitations include fixed oscillator and fixed β parameters, and generality is checked only on a few alternative dynamical systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hypothesizes that dissipative temporal dynamics act as an inductive bias for generalization, tested at representational, structural, and behavioral levels.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Controls phase-space contraction through a single oscillator parameter δ for static inputs and neuron leak β for temporal inputs.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Argues the transition regime trades fit for stability; the authors flag fixed parameters and untested regime generality as limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Concludes that dissipative dynamics are an inductive bias, so generalization may depend on dynamical regime as much as on scale.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists oscillator equations and parameters, a dynamical indicator table, experiment details, Bayesian bound and gradient analyses, and extra figures.

repos.title: TaoMate-FVSR:Audio-Guided Facial Video Restoration
repos.paper_summary:
TaoMate-FVSR is an audio-guided facial video restoration framework for AI-generated video that also supports dubbing under replacement audio. It is a reference-guided flow model built on a Wan video DiT. Reconstruction starts from a mix of the source latent and Gaussian noise (strength 0.80 to 0.95), so the source mouth is not a fixed target. Reference frames and a four-frame motion history enter separate temporal slots. Training has two stages: visual restoration on degraded images and videos, then lip correction on degraded dubbed sources conditioned on target audio, with a SyncNet loss.

On a 150-video talking-head benchmark at 4× downsampling, it reports LPIPS 0.0793 and DISTS 0.0858, versus 0.1380 and 0.1421 for InstantRestore, and Sync-C/Sync-D of 7.413/7.561, versus 6.545/8.170 for SparkVSR. SparkVSR has higher PSNR (30.62 vs 28.67 dB) and SSIM (0.8863 vs 0.8836). On 30 replacement-audio clips, the enhanced-reference variant reaches Sync-C 8.175, versus 7.917 for the best cascade.

Limitations: the main comparison uses the ground-truth first frame as reference, and the enhanced-reference variant lowers PSNR to 23.52 dB. Native AIGC results are qualitative only.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Restoring small AIGC faces requires lip and teeth detail that agrees with the spoken audio, not only sharper pixels.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans facial and video restoration, generative restoration, visual dubbing, and audio-assisted restoration; the authors focus on unreliable mouths.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method mixes source latents with noise to start flow reconstruction and injects sparse references and history into separate temporal slots.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the 150-video benchmark, Ours has the lowest paired perceptual error, while SparkVSR leads pixel-level fidelity.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors state that reconstructed facial detail is a generative estimate, not evidence of true appearance, and raise impersonation risk.

repos.title: RAG-Anything: All-in-One RAG Framework
repos.paper_summary: RAG-Anything is a unified multimodal retrieval-augmented generation framework that builds a dual graph over documents: a cross-modal graph anchored on non-text units (figures, tables, equations) and a text-based graph, merged by entity-name alignment. Retrieval combines graph neighborhood expansion with dense embedding search over entities, relations, and chunks, and a VLM answers using text context plus the dereferenced visual content. On DocBench, it reaches 63.4% overall accuracy versus 61.0% for MMGraphRAG, 58.4% for LightRAG, and 51.2% for GPT-4o-mini. On MMLongBench, it reaches 42.8% versus 38.9% for LightRAG and 37.7% for MMGraphRAG. The gap grows with document length: on DocBench it is over 13 points for documents over 100 pages. Ablations on DocBench show 60.0% for chunk-only retrieval and 62.4% without the reranker, against 63.4% for the full system. All baselines use GPT-4o-mini, and accuracy is judged by GPT-4o-mini. The paper reports no variance across runs. Evaluation covers two benchmarks only.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing RAG systems handle only text, so multimodal documents are poorly served; the paper proposes RAG-Anything to fix this.

digest_headlines.heading: The RAG-Anything Framework
digest_headlines.headline: RAG-Anything decomposes documents into typed units, builds two linked graphs, and retrieves through both structure and embeddings.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On MMLongBench, RAG-Anything scores 42.8% overall versus 37.7% for MMGraphRAG, with gains growing on longer documents.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work groups graph-enhanced RAG and multimodal RAG, and argues that prior multimodal systems fragment by modality.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that dual-graph retrieval helps long documents and identifies text-centric bias and rigid spatial processing as failure modes.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, extra case studies, the three multimodal prompts, the accuracy prompt, and failure-case analyses.

repos.title: RF-DETR: Neural Architecture Search for Real-Time Detection Transformers
repos.paper_summary: RF-DETR is a specialist detection transformer that uses weight-sharing neural architecture search to discover accuracy-latency Pareto curves for target datasets without re-training. The model replaces the LW-DETR backbone with DINOv2 and applies a scheduler-free training procedure. During training, it samples random configurations of image resolution, patch size, windowed attention blocks, decoder layers, and query tokens. At inference, grid search selects specific sub-nets from this single trained model to match hardware constraints. On COCO, RF-DETR (nano) achieves 48.0 AP at 2.3 ms latency, outperforming D-FINE (nano) by 5.3 AP. The 2x-large variant reaches 60.1 AP on COCO, the first real-time detector to exceed 60 AP. On Roboflow100-VL, RF-DETR (2x-large) surpasses GroundingDINO (tiny) by 1.2 AP while running 20 times faster. The paper notes that latency measurements are sensitive to GPU power throttling, proposing a standardized buffering protocol for reproducible benchmarking.

repos.title: Reinforcement Learning for Versatile, Dynamic, and Robust Bipedal Locomotion Control
repos.paper_summary: This paper presents a dual-history reinforcement learning controller for bipedal robots, enabling diverse locomotion skills including walking, running, and jumping on the Cassie robot. The method uses a long-term input/output history encoder to adapt to dynamics changes and contact events, combined with a short-term history fed directly to the policy network to handle high-frequency control needs. Training follows a three-stage curriculum: single-task learning, task randomization, and dynamics randomization. In simulation ablations, the dual-history architecture outperforms baselines like RMA and state-feedback-only policies under randomized dynamics parameters. Real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, with the robot maintaining stable standing for 459 days, completing a 400-meter dash, and executing jumps up to 1.4 meters forward and 0.44 meters high. The authors identify task randomization as a key source of robustness distinct from dynamics randomization, promoting compliant recovery behaviors. Limitations include difficulty achieving precise velocity tracking during fast running and the requirement for specific reference motions; for instance, backward jumps could not be learned from a forward-jumping reference alone.

repos.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
repos.paper_summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a training algorithm that aligns language models with human preferences using a binary cross-entropy loss, eliminating the need for reinforcement learning. DPO derives this objective by reparameterizing the reward function in standard RLHF as $\hat{r}(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}$, where $\pi_\theta$ is the policy being trained and $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is a fixed reference model. This substitution allows the optimal policy to be extracted in closed form from the Bradley-Terry preference model. The paper proves that under mild assumptions, this reparameterization preserves the full class of representable reward functions without loss of generality. Experiments on IMDb sentiment generation, Reddit TL;DR summarization, and Anthropic dialogue tasks show DPO matches or exceeds PPO-based RLHF performance. In sentiment control, DPO achieves higher expected reward at equivalent KL-divergence levels than PPO. For summarization and dialogue, GPT-4 evaluations indicate DPO win rates are comparable to or better than PPO baselines. Limitations include evaluation reliance on GPT-4 judgments and untested scaling beyond 6B parameter models.

repos.title: Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context Attention
repos.paper_summary:
Latent Sparse Attention (LSA) is a sparse attention layer for ultra-long context. It clusters keys in a learned latent space, and each query scores cluster centroids instead of every key. Keys are pooled four to one, grouped into buckets by Ward's agglomerative clustering, and queries pick top buckets (flat search) or descend a tree with beam search (Tree, which is subquadratic in prefill). Attention then runs over sink, window, and selected keys. Distilled-LSA (D-LSA) adds LSA to a frozen pre-trained model by training only small per-layer projections and a temperature against the frozen layer's attention. Native-LSA (N-LSA) is trained on next-token loss alone.

Evaluation uses RULER and PaperTrail, a long-context scientific reading benchmark the authors built. At 10M tokens, one D-LSA attention layer prefills 22.7× and decodes 4.6× faster than sparse attention on GLM-5.3-Flash, and 72.4× and 42.5× faster than full attention on Qwen-3.8-27B, with similar accuracy. N-LSA matches full-attention accuracy with a 1.6× per-layer training speedup at 128k tokens.

Limitations: the KV cache still grows linearly with context, tree search loses accuracy faster than flat search past 1M tokens on GLM-5.3-Flash, and N-LSA was tested only at about 0.5B parameters with flat search.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse attention indexers that score every key dominate cost at ultra-long context, so LSA clusters keys instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Sparse Attention
digest_headlines.headline: At 10M tokens the indexer takes 98% of sparse attention's prefill time, and current indexers still scan every key.

digest_headlines.heading: Latent Sparse Attention (LSA)
digest_headlines.headline: LSA clusters keys in a learned latent space, and each query scores only bucket centroids, flat or as a tree.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: D-LSA keeps accuracy close to baselines up to 10M tokens, and N-LSA matches full-attention validation loss at 128k.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Tree search loses accuracy faster than flat past 1M tokens, and native training was tested only at small scale.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: LSA offers a practical route to ultra-long context attention, through distillation of pre-trained models or native training.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers oracle key-budget tests, method symbols, training data, PaperTrail, evaluation setup, and parallelism details.

repos.title: HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvement for Harness Token Efficiency
repos.paper_summary: HarnessMM reduces repeated reasoning calls in agent harnesses by storing already-resolved actions as executable decision graphs and replaying them when tool feedback satisfies public guards, with recursive self-improvement refining companion harness configurations. A controller sits at the model–tool boundary and keeps model weights fixed. The method reuses stored actions, with literal arguments, causal dependencies and guards, and calls the original actor again when a new semantic decision, unsupported evidence or abstention occurs. On 98 HumanEval tasks, Codex keeps 90.82% success while Tokens/task (k) fall from 66.72 to 47.02 (29.54% saving). DeepSeek Harness rises from 71.43% to 85.71% success while Tokens/task (k) fall from 96.28 to 11.62 (87.93% saving). On MBPP, the Qwen-backed DeepSeek Harness rises from 90.27% to 91.83% with Tokens/task (k) falling from 53.98 to 10.61. The paper's stated limitations are that savings depend on provider cache and context accounting, that new semantic decisions still require slow reasoning, and that public-state adapters are task specific. Small development sets leave policy-level quality differences uncertain.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Harnesses re-invoke reasoning after each tool result, even when earlier reasoning already fixed the next action.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior methods reduce, route or reuse calls, while HarnessMM targets whether a future reasoning call must recur.

digest_headlines.heading: Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: Substitution saves cost only when removed reasoning tokens exceed the tokens introduced by authorship, routing and fallback.

digest_headlines.heading: HarnessMM: Reusing Decisions
digest_headlines.headline: Guarded reuse executes stored actions only when public guards hold, and otherwise returns control to the original actor.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On 98 HumanEval test tasks, HarnessMM keeps Codex success at 90.82% and raises DeepSeek Harness success to 85.71%.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Savings depend on provider accounting and resolved-action availability, and adapters are task specific.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Stored, guard-checked decisions can replace repeated reasoning calls, and companion studies keep their own scope.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives per-iteration MiniWoB++ RSI measurements, development protocols, implementation details and paired-effect definitions.

repos.title: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing
repos.paper_summary: TailSteer is a final-stage training framework that reduces cumulative drift in multi-turn image editing by steering only the late denoising steps of a base editor. The refined model is trained on its own on-policy rollouts, using unchanged source content as a preservation reference, so no curated ground-truth editing pairs are needed. Early steps are trained to match the frozen base model's velocity. Later steps blend that velocity with a preservation velocity toward a source-based endpoint, with the blend weight falling from 1 at the steering onset to 0 at the final step. The method is tested on FLUX.1 Kontext [dev], FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B, SenseNova-U1.5-8B-MoT, and Qwen-Image-2.1. The paper reports substantially reduced drift over 15 to 20 editing turns. On FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B, Qwen-IB EN changes by at most +0.47 across the tested steering onsets. Limitations: drift is measured only over 15 to 20 turns, training uses only identity and local edit families, and qualitative comparisons use one steering onset.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: One-shot editors accumulate small errors across repeated turns, so strong single-turn editing does not guarantee long-horizon editing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior fixes add modules, change representations, or add memory, whereas TailSteer trains the base model's own denoising dynamics.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: TailSteer trains a copy of the base model on its own rollouts, steering only late denoising steps toward source-preserving endpoints.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Across four backbones, TailSteer reduces drift over 15–20 editing turns while keeping single-turn scores close to base models.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion says TailSteer reduces cumulative drift across FLUX, SenseNova, and Qwen while largely retaining base generative capabilities.
